#5453. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:49 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5452. I’ve Worked With 131,201 Entrepreneurs — and 95% of Them Make These 2 Mistakes

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

After helping more than 131,000 business owners, I’ve learned that sustainable growth usually comes down to avoiding two surprisingly common mistakes.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

After nearly 30 years of working with small business owners, you start noticing patterns.

It doesn’t matter whether someone owns a dental practice, a restaurant, a home services company or an ecommerce business. It doesn’t even matter how smart or talented the entrepreneur is. Certain mistakes show up again and again.

I understand why. Running a business means making dozens of decisions every day. The urgent stuff screams for your attention. New ideas are exciting. Cutting expenses feels responsible. And the latest marketing or technology trend can make you wonder whether you’re falling behind.

Meanwhile, the boring fundamentals that actually drive growth are easy to neglect.

I’ve learned that firsthand. I built PostcardMania from scratch starting in 1998, without investors or outside funding, and I’ve made plenty of mistakes along the way — including one that nearly cost me my company.

After working with 131,201 entrepreneurs, though, two mistakes stand out. I see some version of them in roughly 95% of the small business owners I interact with.

Too many entrepreneurs view marketing primarily as an expense to control. I look at it differently: Marketing is the engine that brings customers into your business.

That doesn’t mean spending recklessly. It means knowing your numbers. How much does it cost you to acquire a customer? What is that customer worth over time? Which campaigns consistently generate profitable business?

Once you know those answers, cutting marketing simply because it looks expensive can actually be one of the riskiest things you do.

I learned that during the 2008-09 housing crash and subsequent financial crisis. At the time, 46% of PostcardMania’s clientele was tied to real estate and mortgages. When those industries collapsed, we lost thousands of customers. Revenue dropped, and eventually I began wondering whether we could make payroll.

I refused to lay people off, so advisers suggested cutting our postcard marketing. I reluctantly agreed. It backfired.

Fewer postcards meant fewer leads. Fewer leads meant even less revenue. In 2009, revenue fell 15%. Eventually, I realized that if I wanted revenue to recover, I needed to restore the flow of leads. I brought our marketing budget back to its previous level, and the business recovered.

That experience changed how I think about marketing forever.

So when Covid hit in 2020, and our weekly revenue plunged more than 40%, I did the opposite of 2008: I kept marketing steady. Within five weeks, our weekly revenue had fully recovered and was back above $1 million. Leads rose 9.24% over the next six months without increasing budget. And since then, our revenue has nearly doubled from $60 million annually to nearly $120 million.

Big companies understand that growth requires marketing investment. In August, Kraft Heinz announced they were investing an additional $100 million in its turnaround plan, with most of those funds going toward marketing. The company said it was already seeing stronger performance where those investments were being made.

The lesson for entrepreneurs is simple: If you need more revenue, you need more marketing. Growth requires feeding what works.

Identify your top marketing tactics by measuring revenue and return on investment. From there, ask yourself, “How much more can I responsibly put behind this?”

Entrepreneurs love a shortcut. I do, too. The problem is when the shortcut becomes the strategy.

A new platform appears. An algorithm changes. AI explodes. A marketing hack goes viral. Suddenly everyone feels like they’re falling behind if they aren’t jumping on the bandwagon. But businesses aren’t usually built through a collection of hacks. They’re built by finding things that work and getting exceptionally good at repeating them.

Chili’s is a useful example. The restaurant chain experimented with flashy technology, including robot servers that quickly expanded to 61 locations. The results were disappointing — just a few months later, Chili’s announced it was pulling the plug on its robot initiative.

Instead, they pivoted to a much less “exciting” strategy: fundamentals.

Over the past two years, Chili’s parent company invested in stronger Wi-Fi, updated payment systems and ordering technology for restaurant staff. Its CIO has said every technology initiative now has to contribute to better food service and guest experience.

Meanwhile, Chili’s stock had risen more than 500% between June 2022 and July 2026, with 20 consecutive quarters of same-store sales growth. Of course, those results reflect a turnaround that isn’t just “ditch the robots,” but the philosophy is worth paying attention to: Fix the fundamentals before betting big on flashy tech.

We’ve taken a similar approach at PostcardMania. I’ve watched countless new marketing channels and technologies arrive over the last 28 years, but I’ve never abandoned a strategy simply because something newer came along. Direct mail has essentially built us up into a $120 million company, and it remains a core part of our marketing today. What we’ve done instead is layer newer tools — digital advertising, tracking, automation and programmatic technology — around what was already proven to work.

And the numbers keep validating that decision. We analyzed 117,857 leads in 2025 — every single direct mail and digital lead generated that year — and discovered that we made $416.04 per direct mail lead and only $38.59 per digital lead, a 978% difference.

That doesn’t mean digital is bad. We invest heavily in digital, too. It means you shouldn’t confuse “new” with “better.” It also means you should figure out how new technology can make proven tactics even stronger.

After nearly three decades in business, I’ve become much less impressed by what’s new and much more interested in what works.

Track your marketing. Invest in what produces profitable customers. Keep improving it. Test new ideas without abandoning proven ones. Those principles aren’t flashy, but they’re the bedrock of success.

After nearly 30 years of working with small business owners, you start noticing patterns.

It doesn’t matter whether someone owns a dental practice, a restaurant, a home services company or an ecommerce business. It doesn’t even matter how smart or talented the entrepreneur is. Certain mistakes show up again and again.

I understand why. Running a business means making dozens of decisions every day. The urgent stuff screams for your attention. New ideas are exciting. Cutting expenses feels responsible. And the latest marketing or technology trend can make you wonder whether you’re falling behind.

#5451. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5450. Would You Pay $18 to Get Costco’s $1.50 Hot Dog Combo Delivered to Your Door? This New App Is Betting You’ll Bite.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Costco’s food court offering is famous for its low price, but a new delivery app is inflating the bill for convenience.

Costco sells its hot dog and drink combo for $1.50. A delivery app is betting that getting it delivered and brought to your door is worth a much bigger bill.

According to a recent report from media site SFGate, there’s a new food delivery service in town that promises to bring Costco food court items straight to customers. The platform, called No Tip, is a new service based in Southern California. The mastermind behind it is Jack Chen, a longtime software engineer.

The process is simple. Customers order what they want from Costco’s food court menu through No Tip. Someone will physically go to Costco, wait in line, pick up the food and deliver it. Chen promises to refund customers if their food arrives late — and says the fees are all-inclusive, so no need to pay a tip or added fees.

However, customers are certainly paying extra for convenience.

A whole pizza that costs members $9.95 at the food court runs $30 through No Tip, while the $7.99 rotisserie chicken chef salad jumps to $28 on Chen’s menu. But the biggest sticker shock belongs to Costco’s famous $1.50 hot dog-and-drink combo: No Tip charges $18 to bring it to your door. That’s a 1,100% markup.

Chen defended No Tip’s prices. He told SFGate that he built the site to feed a crowd, not just someone craving a hot dog for lunch — though he will take that order too.

Chen says No Tip’s sweet spot is office lunches, birthday parties and big family dinners. The service is suited for situations where paying for delivery means avoiding a trip across town with a trunk full of pizzas.

“A lot of offices are ordering from me,” Chen said in a phone interview with SFGate. “It’s the company’s money. As long as you’re not too expensive, I mean, they’ve got the money to blow.”

The company also benefits when customers crave Costco food court items over other brands. “You’d be surprised how some people are just craving it specifically,” Chen said.

No Tip is capable of accommodating groups of up to 200 people and includes plates and forks with delivery. It is up to the host to set up and serve the food. A company ordering 200 hot dogs would have to pay $18 for each one.

Chen is personally handling some deliveries and has brought on friends and “some guys” he pays “on the side right now” to help with orders. He wants to eventually add in-house drivers.

Chen created No Tip two months ago and claims that the service stretches across all of Southern California through 66 fulfillment locations.

He had the idea when he was living near Venice Beach and wanted Costco pizza for dinner one night. Getting that pizza meant making the trip to Costco and braving food court lines. Chen then had the idea to eliminate the hassle of getting Costco food court items by offering delivery. He bet that other Costco fans would also pay extra to have their favorites delivered.

“I know my friends have paid, like, $30-plus dollars for some terrible Domino’s in the past,” he said. “So why not try to do this?”

#5449. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

#5446. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5445. What CEOs Need to Know About Deepfakes, Disinformation and the New Rules of Brand Defense

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Learn why CEOs must prioritize brand resilience and build proactive reputation infrastructure before a crisis strikes.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Can your crisis management team keep up with a convincing CEO deepfake that goes viral? Can your reputation (and enterprise value) weather a coordinated cyberattack designed to blow up in public?

Today’s brand threats aren’t easy to identify or predict. They can come from hacker groups, state actors and foreign adversaries, or even just a troll with Claude and a vendetta.

A few years ago, brand reputation risk was much simpler. A stronger competitor. A recession. A product recall. Wars didn’t paint brands as legitimate cyber targets. Coordinated disinformation, leaks and deepfakes weren’t the norm. Today, these are the tools of influence, and corporate reputation is their target.

Add to that the power of AI, which allows false narratives to go global in seconds. When those narratives become embedded in answer engines, they can shape how millions of people perceive your company.

The only way forward is brand resilience. Defending against evolving threats is no longer an IT issue or a crisis communications exercise — it’s a leadership responsibility.

The problem is that most enterprises were never built to manage reputation this way. They have crisis plans, communications teams, cybersecurity infrastructure and brand strategies, but little infrastructure for continuously understanding and protecting their reputation across search engines and AI.

CEOs must invest in building the infrastructure to protect their reputation before a crisis occurs.

“It can’t happen to us.” Famous last words.

With digital attacks, AI abuse or deepfakes, the question isn’t if it will happen. It’s when. The biggest brands and leaders are, ironically, easy marks for disinformation, extortion and theft.  If someone with an AI account and a smartphone can taint executive credibility and even harm enterprise value, imagine what a sophisticated adversary can achieve.

It’s already played out in the headlines. A cyberattack against Stryker splashed across headlines worldwide after an Iran-affiliated group targeted the healthcare giant. That attack wasn’t targeting infrastructure as much as brand credibility and market trust.

Stakeholders were left wondering, “Can I trust Stryker and its leaders with my information?”

What about the Warren Buffett deepfake scam? This time last year, several videos supposedly featuring Buffett were posted to TikTok and YouTube, most notably one with the deceivingly convincing title “Warren Buffett: The #1 Investment Tip For Everyone Over 50 (MUST WATCH).”

The deepfake used Buffett’s image, voice and reputation to make crypto scams appear credible. The result was serious damage to Berkshire Hathaway’s brand credibility and the legacy Buffett had spent decades building.

Generative AI search tools ingest all the available information about a subject. This means during reputation incidents or brand attacks, AI boosts the damage and reach.

It hands attackers a megaphone, reaching social media users with critical content, flipping and remixing scandals into instantly viral narratives. When the LLMs scan the content, it’s hard to course-correct, and the lifespan of any controversy is lengthened.

When you lack owned content or have next to no digital footprint, your brand is at the highest risk. You can’t push back on damaging narratives. That lost authority leaves you at the mercy of coordinated attacks and ensuing noise.

You could call it algorithmic vulnerability. When your brand hasn’t proactively laid a foundation of verified, AI-readable truth, platforms like AI Mode and ChatGPT will default to the dominant narrative. The one controlled by your adversaries.

Beyond narrative threats, there’s also a major market shift happening fast. Agile, tech-savvy companies now pose a direct competitive threat to risk-averse legacy brands.

Anduril ($61B valuation), Revolut ($115B valuation), Anthropic, Canva and OpenAI are challenging the status quo across defense, banking, enterprise software and digital infrastructure.

Establishment players, including tech brands like Apple, face new volatility from new competitors on top of the AI-driven one.

Leaders must shift to a proactive mindset and adopt new priorities — like positioning and narrative, digital defense and the asset landscape. It’s the only way they can mitigate the next inevitable controversy, attack or competitive challenge.

In short, reputation management has to become a fixed enterprise capability, not something activated when a problem appears.

Brand resilience rests on owning your narrative in the spaces that matter most: AI search and organic search. It’s also about planning before a crisis strikes. Here’s how CEOs can take action.

First, you need to know where you are. Analyze, manage and monitor your brand’s digital spaces, including sentiment, gaps, vulnerabilities and opportunities.

Identify the big issues first, like negative news cycles or online attacks. Then get a full picture of existing sentiment and find the gaps that have allowed problems to emerge. This analysis reveals insight into overall brand health, preparedness and resilience.

Begin getting ahead of the news cycle, cyber actors and competitors. Create and launch content assets to build a strong digital presence that can withstand sudden, coordinated smear campaigns.

For example, publish consistent, high-quality thought leadership. This shares brand expertise and builds leadership credibility and the assets needed to drive your true narrative. It also builds your reservoir of trust, increasing controlled visibility that you can rely on when controversy strikes.

Deploy technology to monitor and scale your digital footprint faster than adversaries can manipulate it, building a consistent, authoritative narrative.

But scale shouldn’t mean mass-producing AI content. AI-generated errors and hallucinations can create reputational risks themselves, and Google penalizes “scaled content abuse.” Instead, prioritize human-led content production, augmented by AI.

Together, these efforts create a digital moat that absorbs reputational shocks, strengthens brand resilience and prevents third parties from drowning out your own narrative.

AI came, AI saw, and AI transformed how brand and leader reputations are created and destroyed.

Proactively creating, managing and protecting your brand’s narrative isn’t some marketing fad — it’s a critical requirement for enterprise survival.

Leaders can adapt to the rapid change by investing in their future or risk everything and succumb to complacency. I do not recommend the latter.

Can your crisis management team keep up with a convincing CEO deepfake that goes viral? Can your reputation (and enterprise value) weather a coordinated cyberattack designed to blow up in public?

Today’s brand threats aren’t easy to identify or predict. They can come from hacker groups, state actors and foreign adversaries, or even just a troll with Claude and a vendetta.

A few years ago, brand reputation risk was much simpler. A stronger competitor. A recession. A product recall. Wars didn’t paint brands as legitimate cyber targets. Coordinated disinformation, leaks and deepfakes weren’t the norm. Today, these are the tools of influence, and corporate reputation is their target.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 10, 2026 at 11:58 am

Plaid is opening an engineering office in Seattle’s Westlake neighborhood in January and plans to double its local workforce to about 80 people by next summer.

The San Francisco-based fintech company says the new 11,466-square-foot space at 1000 Dexter Ave. N. will serve as a hub for its technical teams, with most open Seattle roles focused on machine learning, data science and engineering.

Plaid said in a blog post that it chose Seattle because much of the cloud and AI technology behind modern financial infrastructure was built in the region. The company is developing AI models trained on its network to understand patterns in how money moves.

Plaid already has about 40 employees in the Seattle area, who currently work remotely, The Seattle Times reported. “There’s just great talent in Seattle, so it’s a little bit of a no-brainer for us,” Meghan Welch, Plaid’s chief people officer, told the Times.

Plaid’s careers page lists more than 50 open roles that include Seattle as a possible location, though most are also open in San Francisco, New York or other cities. About half are in data, engineering or security, with the rest spread across sales, legal, finance and other teams.

Founded in 2013, Plaid was valued at $8 billion in an employee share sale earlier this year, down from a 2021 peak of $13.4 billion. The company says more than 150 million people have used its technology to connect their financial accounts.

Plaid is led by co-founder and CEO Zachary Perret.

The new office will have views of Lake Union, an outdoor deck and event space, along with three catered meals a day, according to the company.

#5443. The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: AI, Defense And Space Tech Lead For Large Rounds

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

This week brought another plethora of large funding rounds for startups and growth-stage companies. Shield AI, a defense tech player focused on autonomy and virtual simulations, secured the largest financing, bringing in $2 billion. Next on the list was drone delivery provider Zipline International, which pulled in a fresh $1.5 billion.

Rounding out the ranks were good-sized financings for sectors including agentic AI, space tech and AI infrastructure.

1. Shield AI, $2B, defense tech: Shield AI, a developer of autonomy software and systems for the defense sector, along with simulation and synthetic reality technologies, secured $2 billion in equity funding and $500 million in debt financing. The equity included a $1 billion Series H led by Disruptive and Innovation X Capital along with a $1 billion structured equity investment from funds managed by Blackstone. The $500 million debt financing was led by JPMorganChase. San Diego-based Shield also said it is acquiring radar company Echodyne in a transaction valued at $5.3 billion.

2. Zipline International, $1.5B, drones: Drone delivery provider Zipline International raised $1.5 billion in late-stage funding at a $21.5 billion post-money valuation. Paradigm, WCM Investment Management and Layer Global led the financing for the South San Francisco, California-based company, which plans to use the money to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and increase hiring as it builds a nationwide drone delivery network.

3. CesiumAstro, $730M, space tech: Austin-based CesiumAstro, a developer of space and defense communications systems and satellites, closed on $730 million in Series D financing at a valuation of more than $4.5 billion. Janus Henderson led the equity round, and the company also secured $100 million in debt financing through the Export-Import Bank of the United States and JP Morgan.

4. Northwood Space, $375M, space tech: Torrance, California-based Northwood Space, a developer of ground infrastructure to support satellite systems, picked up $375 million in Series C funding. Andreessen Horowitz and DFJ Growth led the financing for the 3-year-old startup, which raised its Series B about nine months ago.

5. Applied Compute, $350M, AI models: Applied Compute, provider of a cloud computing platform that enterprises and developers use to train and run large AI models, announced $350 million in new funding at a $3.25 billion valuation. Elad Gil led the financing, joined by a long list of investors including Nvidia. The San Francisco-based company, which launched 18 months ago, said its annual recurring revenue has already topped $100 million.

6. Harbinger, $240M, electric trucks: Harbinger, a startup known for electric truck technology that has been expanding into battery storage and defense applications, secured $240 million in Series D funding. Tiger Global, Capricorn Investment Group and Ridgeline led the financing for the Garden Grove, California-based company.

7. Sentra, $150M, AI data security: Sentra, a provider of agentic data security tools, closed on $150 million in a strategic investment led by Capital One Ventures. Founded in 2021, Sentra has headquarters in New York and Tel Aviv.

8. Traversal, $120M, agentic AI: Traversal, a startup building AI agents for enterprise site reliability engineering, secured $120 million in new funding at a $1 billion valuation. Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint and Khosla Ventures co-led the round for the New York-based startup.

9. Ocient, $100M, agentic AI: Chicago-based Ocient, a provider of agentic AI for enterprise with a focus on data analytics, picked up $100 million in Series C funding co-led by BOKA Capital and OCA Ventures.

10. (tied) Tutor Intelligence, $75M, robotics: Watertown, Massachusetts-based Tutor Intelligence, a startup focused on robot foundation model training and building robot workers, raised $75 million in Series B funding led by Andreessen Horowitz.

10. (tied) Kalepa, $75M, insurtech: Kalepa, a provider of AI tools for the insurance industry, secured $75 million in Series B funding at a $470 million valuation. Updata Partners led the round for the New York-based startup.

#5442. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5441. From Working the Drive-Thru at Wendy’s to Becoming the CEO of EBONY — Eden Bridgeman Shares the Lessons That Built Her Leadership Style

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

EBONY CEO Eden Bridgeman explains how her franchise background and her father’s leadership lessons are helping her take an 80-year-old cultural institution into the future of media.

Eden Bridgeman began her working life with shifts at Wendy’s and Chili’s—jobs that taught her key lessons on a career path that put her in the driver’s seat of one of the most iconic brands in media history.

Bridgeman went on from working behind the counter to becoming the CMO of Manna, Inc., a restaurant franchise operator. And in 2021, after her father, the late Ulysses “Junior” Bridgeman, bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020, she took the reins of EBONY.

This fall, EBONY unveiled its 2026 Power 100 list, a class that stretches from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator, all celebrated at a gala at the Hollywood Palladium under the theme “The Stories We Shape.” One of the categories, the Junior Bridgeman Business Vanguard, is named in her father’s honor.

Following the event, Bridgeman shared her thoughts on leadership that serves your team, finding success in the attention economy and defining power that truly makes an impact.

As a teenager, you worked at Wendy’s and Chili’s. What is one specific habit or rule from those shifts that you still use as a CEO? One thing I learned very early is that the customer experiences the whole business, not your department. If something was wrong with an order, the customer did not care whether the mistake happened at the register, in the kitchen, or somewhere else. They simply knew the experience did not meet their expectations. Working in restaurants teaches you very quickly that everyone has some responsibility for the final outcome. Restaurants also taught me the importance of staying close to the business. You learn things from the front line that you cannot always see in a report.

You were CMO of a restaurant franchise operator, and then took over an 80-year old media brand. What surprised you most about the media business? Honestly, how many businesses exist inside of the media business. Coming from restaurants, there were certainly complexities, but the economic model was relatively clear. Media has a very different ecosystem. You have the audience consuming the product, advertisers funding parts of the business, platforms influencing distribution, creators and talent shaping relevance, technology affecting discovery, and increasingly commerce and experiences creating additional revenue opportunities. All of those constituencies matter, but they do not always want the same thing.

That requires a different kind of discipline. One of the biggest lessons for me has been that attention and revenue are not the same thing. A piece of content can perform extremely well culturally and still not create meaningful business value unless you have built the right infrastructure around that attention.

What practices from the restaurant world do you think can apply to success in media? There are actually quite a few. The first is frequency. Restaurants understand that growth is not just about convincing somebody to visit once. The second is consistency. In restaurants, brand standards exist because people expect a certain experience every time they walk through the door. Media brands need that same clarity. And then there is measurement. Restaurant businesses are incredibly disciplined about understanding performance at a granular level. You know what is selling, when it is selling and where there are operational problems. I bring that mindset to EBONY because I believe creativity becomes more powerful when you understand its impact.

Your father bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020. When you took over in 2021, what were the first things you fixed or rebuilt? I tend to be careful with the word “fixed,” because it can suggest that everything before you was wrong. That is not how I view EBONY. We inherited an extraordinary brand with generations of cultural equity, but the business around that brand had to operate in a fundamentally different media environment. So much of my focus has been on rebuilding the infrastructure necessary for EBONY to compete as a modern media company. That means strengthening how we operate, how we sell, how we develop partnerships, how we think about content and distribution, and how we measure whether the work is producing the outcomes we intended.

But there was also a more philosophical question that had to be answered: What does it mean to modernize EBONY without disconnecting it from what made it important in the first place? There are generations of people who have a personal relationship with this brand. Then there is a younger generation whose relationship with media, culture and identity is completely different. My responsibility is not to choose between those audiences. It is to understand the fundamental truth that made EBONY matter historically and translate that truth into products, experiences and storytelling that feel relevant now. Legacy gives you permission to enter the conversation. Relevance determines whether people continue listening.

Are there any leadership lessons or words of encouragement from your father that you think about regularly? I would describe it less as one particular quote and more as a leadership philosophy I learned from my father: the inverted pyramid.

The idea is that leadership is not about positioning yourself at the top with everyone working up toward you. You turn the pyramid upside down. As a leader, your responsibility is to support the people doing the work and make sure they have what they need to be successful.

That has stayed with me because it changes the way you think about leadership. A title may give you authority, but leadership is really about service, accountability and creating the conditions for other people to succeed.

As CEO, I try to remember that my role is not to have every answer or to be the center of every decision. My responsibility is to provide clarity around where we are going, remove obstacles where I can, make the difficult decisions when necessary, and give the team the support and accountability they need to do their best work.

I think that philosophy takes on another layer at EBONY. There is a responsibility to the people working to move the business forward, but also to the audience and community that have trusted this brand for generations.

The higher you move in an organization, the more people you are responsible for serving, not the more people who are responsible for serving you.

My father led humbly, as a servant leader, and that is the lesson from him I carry most directly into how I try to lead today.

Where do you think are the biggest opportunities for EBONY and other legacy media brands in today’s media landscape? I think the biggest opportunity is to stop defining a media company primarily by the content it publishes. Content will always be essential, but it can extend into original intellectual property, experiences, commerce, recommendations, partnerships and new forms of distribution. It can create opportunities for brands that want genuine cultural credibility. And it gives us the ability to convene communities both digitally and physically.

I also believe there is significant opportunity in understanding audiences more deeply. Our history is an enormous competitive advantage, but history cannot become an excuse for standing still. Younger consumers are not obligated to love EBONY because their parents or grandparents did. We have to earn their relationship with the brand on their terms.

If we can combine the trust and cultural authority built over generations with the technology, formats, distribution and business models available today, I think the opportunity is much larger than traditional publishing.

The Power 100 honorees range from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator. How do you define “power”?

I think power has become much more distributed. Traditionally, we tended to associate power with institutions: the person running the company, controlling capital, holding political office or deciding who gained access. Those forms of power still matter enormously. But technology and social platforms have created entirely different ways for people to build influence.

A young person can create something from their bedroom and develop an audience larger than many traditional media outlets. A creator can introduce millions of people to an idea, product or cause almost instantly. An entrepreneur can build a community without first receiving permission from a traditional gatekeeper.

That changes the way we should think about power. For EBONY, I think power is ultimately about the ability to create meaningful impact. Can you shift a conversation? Can you open a door that was previously closed? Can you build something that creates opportunity for other people? Can you influence how people see themselves or what they believe is possible? When I think about power today, I am interested not only in who has it, but what they are doing with it.

Eden Bridgeman began her working life with shifts at Wendy’s and Chili’s—jobs that taught her key lessons on a career path that put her in the driver’s seat of one of the most iconic brands in media history.

Bridgeman went on from working behind the counter to becoming the CMO of Manna, Inc., a restaurant franchise operator. And in 2021, after her father, the late Ulysses “Junior” Bridgeman, bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020, she took the reins of EBONY.

This fall, EBONY unveiled its 2026 Power 100 list, a class that stretches from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator, all celebrated at a gala at the Hollywood Palladium under the theme “The Stories We Shape.” One of the categories, the Junior Bridgeman Business Vanguard, is named in her father’s honor.

#5440. Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:48 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:27 am

The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September.

Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill, which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.

Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”

The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.

That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.

“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September, the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported.

Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”

Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

#5439. Paper Unicorns Are Cheap. Building A $1B Revenue AI Company Takes A Multimarket Cap Table

A $1 billion valuation still makes a startup a unicorn on paper. Yet when 250 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in the first half of 2026, the speed of wealth creation raised another question: How many of these businesses can keep their customers once the initial excitement fades?

I would set a higher benchmark for unicorns with $1 billion in revenue sustained by customers who keep paying.

I spent five years at Harbin Institute of Technology and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, where “fail fast, improve faster” shaped my approach to building technology. Having studied in China before building an AI company in Abu Dhabi, I have also seen how the same growth story can raise different questions among investors, eventually boiling down to: “What will customers keep paying for?”

Fast revenue deserves attention. Founders who turn pilots into paying deployments are solving a real problem, and strong sales can make the next round easier. An annualized run rate built from discounts, experimental budgets or generous compute subsidies, however, offers little assurance that customers will stay.

Since 2023, the price of hitting a fixed level of AI performance has dropped thirteenfold every year. Startups that just resell model access now face brutal price competition. Look at OpenRouter and its $113 million Series B: developers can already swap between models through one shared interface.

Businesses built around proprietary workflows face a different test. Software embedded in a company’s approvals, records and daily decisions can be far harder to replace than the model doing the underlying work. I would check whether customers renew at full price and expand their contracts. Then I would see whether margins stay healthy after inference costs.

Once founders know who keeps buying, they should raise across regions, because a local backer can double as market entry. Borders barely slow an AI product down. Enterprise sales still depend on local budgets, procurement procedures and relationships. A foreign investor becomes valuable when those connections turn a product demonstration into a paid contract.

The $30 million Series A for London- and Gulf-based 1001 AI offers a useful example. U.S. venture firm Lux Capital led the financing, alongside Saudi PIF-backed Sanabil Investments. The deal cannot establish future retention by itself, but it shows how capital, talent and customers can sit on different maps, with engineers in London and customers in the Gulf.

Ask every investor what they bring besides money. One warm introduction to the right buyer can beat a higher valuation if it turns into a contract you can actually deliver and renew.

The choice between traditional venture funding and sovereign-backed money is often framed as a choice between fast and patient capital. I find the more practical distinction lies in the obligations attached to each check.

In conversations with U.S. and European venture investors, I have often been asked how quickly we could turn product adoption into repeatable sales before competitors caught up.

Venture firms need returns within their fund’s life. That puts commercial momentum and a sizable exit at the center of their investment decisions. The pressure can sharpen execution. It can also backfire when founders who chase fast expansion without counting delivery costs may fill their pipeline with discounted experiments instead of enduring enterprise relationships.

Sovereign-backed investors usually ask me a very different set of questions. They want to know where user data gets processed and which technical capabilities stay in the country. Will local customers still be able to rely on the service years from now?

Some funds carry an explicit domestic development mandate. For them, those concerns can count as investment criteria alongside financial returns. The upside is a partner who cares about local infrastructure and enterprise adoption. The price can be longer diligence and localization spending. Contract terms that make it harder to expand elsewhere can also cause a problem.

Neither mandate is universal. Many sovereign-backed funds pursue conventional financial returns, while traditional VCs can support long enterprise sales cycles. Government-affiliated capital doesn’t guarantee procurement wins, either.

Founders should read the fine print: governance rights, exclusivity requests, promised commercial introductions. Then judge whether the investor’s regional reach is worth the constraints.

The best capital strategy follows the customer’s path, from a working product to a renewal. Venture money speeds up development and sales once the business model works. Regional strategic investors earn their place when a new market’s infrastructure and procurement rules call for local expertise.

I would rather show an investor a small cohort of customers renewing without discounts than a glossy revenue forecast that depends on the next funding round. The numbers to watch are net revenue retention, production deployments and margins after delivery costs.

Market sentiment will keep minting and erasing paper unicorns every quarter. The founding teams that build $1 billion in lasting annual revenue will likely balance venture momentum with regional obligations. Their global cap tables will mirror the enterprise markets they serve.

Ilman Shazhaev is the founder and CEO of Dizzaract, an AI and gaming infrastructure company headquartered in Abu Dhabi and the largest game development studio in the Middle East. His work focuses on distributed AI infrastructure, human behavioral data and the interactive environments in which AI systems are trained and tested. Shazhaev is a United Nations expert under the UNODC program, advising on how AI can help solve social problems in developing economies. He is also the author of 46 scientific articles, including published research on AI that reads a player’s psychological state from ordinary gaming hardware, and holds 10 registered invention patents.

#5438. 3 Ways Businesses Can Create Lasting Value Across Borders

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From building relationships to adapting to local markets, lasting growth depends on more than simply expanding a company’s reach.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Asia has undergone an extraordinary economic transformation over the past several decades. Countries that once played relatively modest roles in international commerce have become important centers of manufacturing, technology, finance and innovation.

What interests me most about this transformation is not simply the speed of growth, but the way businesses across the region have learned to operate in markets with very different cultures, languages and economic conditions.

Consider Southeast Asia. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment into the region reached $226 billion in 2024, an increase of 8% even as global investment flows declined. The region has become an important part of international supply chains, connecting businesses and customers across Asia and beyond.

Yet Asia is not a single market. Doing business in Singapore is very different from doing business in Vietnam, Indonesia or Japan. Each has its own expectations, regulations and ways of building relationships.

I believe this diversity is precisely what makes Asia such an interesting place from which to learn. For entrepreneurs looking to expand internationally, three lessons stand out.

In many parts of Asia, business relationships are built gradually. People want to understand who they are dealing with, whether they can rely on them and whether there is a genuine commitment to working together.

This is not unique to Asia, of course, but it is particularly relevant in a region where business practices and cultural expectations can vary considerably between countries.

When entering a new market, entrepreneurs naturally focus on commercial opportunities. They study demand, calculate potential returns and consider how quickly they can establish operations. These are important questions, but they should not come at the expense of understanding people.

The Asian Development Bank’s Asian Economic Integration Report 2025 examines how regional cooperation, investment and participation in global value chains have helped shape Asia’s economic development.

Behind these economic relationships are businesses that must learn to work together across borders. Reliable partnerships, mutual understanding and the ability to resolve differences are essential to making that cooperation successful.

I have always believed that trust is built through consistency. People remember whether we honor our commitments, communicate honestly and treat them fairly when difficulties arise.

A partnership may begin with a commercial agreement, but its strength is often tested when circumstances change. Markets can become uncertain, costs can rise, and plans do not always unfold as expected.

For entrepreneurs, the lesson is to resist the temptation to treat relationships simply as a means of entering a market. Take time to understand local expectations, listen carefully and choose partners whose values are compatible with your own.

The strongest relationships are often those that continue long after the first transaction has been completed.

One of the most valuable lessons from Asia is that geographical proximity does not necessarily mean cultural or commercial similarity.

A business that succeeds in Singapore cannot assume that the same approach will work in Thailand or Indonesia. Consumer preferences, purchasing habits, regulations and expectations of service can differ significantly. This makes Asia an excellent reminder that international expansion requires flexibility.

The OECD’s 2026 Digital Trade Review of ASEAN highlights both the region’s growing digital opportunities and the regulatory differences that continue to complicate cross-border business.

The report estimates that ASEAN’s digital trade exports have reached $387 billion, representing nearly 20% of the region’s total exports. At the same time, differences in national regulations and cross-border data requirements remain obstacles to deeper integration.

For businesses, the implications are clear. Technology may make it easier to reach customers in another country, but it does not eliminate the need to understand how that market operates.

I believe successful international businesses distinguish between the principles they should preserve and the practices they should be willing to change.

A company’s commitment to quality, integrity and customer service should remain consistent wherever it operates. But how those commitments are delivered may need to be adapted to local circumstances.

This requires listening to local employees and customers rather than assuming that decisions made at headquarters will always be appropriate. It also requires humility. Entrepreneurs need confidence in their ideas, but they must remain willing to acknowledge when something is not working.

Sometimes the wisest decision is to test a smaller opportunity, learn from the response and adjust before committing substantial resources.

Asia’s diversity reminds us that successful expansion is not about imposing the same formula everywhere. It is about understanding what people value and finding a way to meet their needs without compromising what the business stands for.

Perhaps the most important lesson from Asia’s economic development is the value of investing in people, skills and long-term capabilities.

Many of the region’s economies have developed through participation in international production networks. Businesses do not necessarily manufacture an entire product in one country. Instead, different stages of production take place across several markets, drawing on specialized skills and resources.

The ASEAN Investment Report 2025 highlights how investment has supported the development of regional supply chains in industries including semiconductors, automotive manufacturing and apparel.

This is significant because international investment can contribute more than capital. When supported by training, knowledge-sharing and strong local partnerships, it can help businesses and workers develop capabilities that remain valuable over time.

For entrepreneurs, I believe there is an important distinction between establishing operations in another country and becoming a meaningful part of its economy.

A business may open an office, hire employees and begin generating revenue. But if every important decision is made elsewhere and local people have few opportunities to develop, its long-term contribution may be limited.

By contrast, businesses that invest in training, develop local leaders and encourage the exchange of knowledge can create stronger foundations for growth.

This does not require a large organization or an elaborate program. Smaller businesses can provide mentoring, professional development and opportunities for employees to take on greater responsibility.

These investments may not deliver immediate financial returns, but they help build the experience and confidence that organizations need as they grow.

I also believe there is something important about creating opportunities that extend beyond the business itself. When people acquire new skills, they carry that knowledge throughout their careers. Their development can benefit other organizations, industries and communities.

Asia’s experience demonstrates the potential of economies working together while developing their own capabilities. Entrepreneurs everywhere can learn from that approach.

Asia’s economic success has not followed a single model. Different countries have developed their own strengths, and the region continues to face challenges involving trade, regulation and economic uncertainty. Nevertheless, its experience offers useful lessons for businesses seeking opportunities beyond their home markets.

Relationships require patience. Local differences deserve respect. And lasting growth depends on developing people and capabilities, not simply increasing sales.

There will always be pressure to expand quickly, particularly when competitors appear to be moving ahead. But entering more markets is not necessarily the same as building a stronger business.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to consider not only where their next opportunity might be, but also what they can contribute when they get there. Can they become trusted partners? Can they serve customers in ways that reflect local needs? Can they create opportunities for people to learn and grow?

These questions may not produce the fastest route to expansion, but they encourage a more sustainable approach to international business.

To me, the greatest lesson from Asia is that creating value across borders requires more than the movement of goods, services and capital. It requires an understanding of people and a willingness to build relationships that endure.

Businesses that recognize this have an opportunity to achieve something more meaningful than international reach. They can create lasting value wherever they operate.

Asia has undergone an extraordinary economic transformation over the past several decades. Countries that once played relatively modest roles in international commerce have become important centers of manufacturing, technology, finance and innovation.

What interests me most about this transformation is not simply the speed of growth, but the way businesses across the region have learned to operate in markets with very different cultures, languages and economic conditions.

Consider Southeast Asia. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment into the region reached $226 billion in 2024, an increase of 8% even as global investment flows declined. The region has become an important part of international supply chains, connecting businesses and customers across Asia and beyond.
